utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The court is back in session. If you would please bring in the accused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What about our interpreters, operational? So what about the interpreters, can they hear me? Office of the Prosecutor, you hear me? Mr. Blaskic, the Defence, everybody can hear me, fellow judges? Great. Mr. Harmon is here too now. Mr. Harmon is going to tell us how this is going to be unfolding this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. President, your Honours, counsel. Mr. President, we intended this afternoon's session to present two witnesses to your Honours, but unfortunately, one of the witnesses who arrived late last night and who was being prepared for this afternoon's testimony became ill around noon and is unable to proceed with her testimony. I regret that, both for her and for the court and its desire to expedite these proceedings. We will be calling one witness this afternoon, the witness is a protected witness and will be identified as Witness L, and the examination of Witness L will be conducted by my new colleague, Ms. Nancy Paterson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So on behalf of fellow judges and myself, we welcome Nancy Paterson, now a new lawyer, new form of examination, so that is always good news, as it were. Mr. Hayman might perhaps like to say a few words. You do not mind the protective measures I assume, even though perhaps you were not informed of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We were informed, your Honour, this afternoon, by the court staff. We have no objection. I would like to welcome Ms. Paterson on behalf of the Defence, but note we are not getting a transcript on our monitors. May I just enquire if the other parties of the court are getting a reading of the transcript on their monitors?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is right. There is no transcript whatever, you are quite right, Mr. Hayman. We need those transcripts, that is our memory, so Registrar, what can you do for us?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: In fact they are not on the screen but they are out there, they do exist, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is not really a satisfactory answer, I am afraid.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I will check up on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There you go. You really have a way of getting things done, Registrar, you just need to move a little bit and it falls into place. So is it Peterson or Paterson? Here we go. Nancy Paterson. So madam, as said you are more than welcome. Now, we have worked out this new method, as you probably know, last week. You are going to start by telling us how long you plan on examining your witness for, what your forecast is, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We anticipate this witness will take approximately one hour, or an hour and a half, but probably not any more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. Now as fellow judges and myself have decided, we ask for a brief account. When I say a brief account, what I mean is not to tell us everything the witness is going to be telling us, that would be pointless, what is important is that you focus on the key points in connection with the charges against General Blaskic, the points that fit into your strategy, what your expectations are, what this witness is going to be contributing, so you do not have to be long about it. On the contrary, you can just tell us "this witness is important to us for this, that and the other reason", and that way, the court can ensure that the Prosecution -- and then one day it will be for the Defence to play by the same rules -- can go down that tack. I am sure you are familiar with what we are looking for. In the course of the status conference, we will take stock of this, but the day before yesterday I think that we gained considerable time, if I dare say so, as compared with the anticipations of the Prosecution. Of course, considerably this does not change anything, but for the judges, this enables us to be even more vigilant in following exactly the key elements of the hearing. So please tell us very briefly what the key focus is going to be here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This is another civilian witness who was a resident of the village of Ahmici on 16th April 1993. She will be telling the court about the experiences of herself and her family. She will describe her experiences as she and her family had to flee from their house because of the advancing troops that they had seen, the fires and destruction in the village. She will describe for you the unfortunate event when she herself was shot, from behind, by forces in the village. She will describe how her mother was shot and killed close to where she was shot and will describe how she was rescued from that location, and finally she will describe the death of some additional family members. But because of the reason of her anonymity, we will ask that part of her testimony at the end be done in a private session, so that she can discuss more openly the names of some of the family members which we do not feel she can do in open court. But that will be a very short part of her testimony at the very conclusion of her testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine, thank you. Registrar, perhaps we could bring in Witness L.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Witness L? Now Witness L, we are going to verify your identity. Do not tell us what your name is, we just want you to look at the name we have written down, but you need not say anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good. Now the usher is going to provide you -- or the Registrar will be presenting you with the solemn oath. Go right ahead. WITNESS L (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness L, at the Prosecutor's request, you have received protective measures, very strict protective measures, and that means that you can speak freely, without any fear, before the International Tribunal, and it is for us to try General Blaskic, who is in the courtroom here. Now, the procedure is going to work as follows. There is going to be some quick identification, but that will be very quick indeed, as you are a protected witness, that is to say a witness who is not to be identified. You will address the court directly, and you will tell us what you witnessed, starting from 16th April 1993, going straight to the essential things you have to say, without getting tied up in details, but while saying what you have to say. Now, the Prosecution may occasionally interrupt you for additional questions, then there will be some additional questions to clarify certain points, it is just going to be a matter of clarifying a few things and after that it will be the counsel for the Defence, one of the counsel for the Defence, who will be putting questions for you, because this is an International Tribunal and we do want to hear what you have to say. Please, Ms. Paterson, go right ahead. First it is just a matter of some preliminary information, otherwise the witness can go straight into her narrative.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just to clarify, the witness is going to speak briefly about a few events which occurred before 16th April, but most of her testimony will focus on 16th April. Witness L, were you a resident of the village of Ahmici in Bosnia-Herzegovina on 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: How old were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Did you live with your family in that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Would you explain to the court, without saying the names, who the members of your family were that were living with you at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My father, my mother, two sisters, brother, my sister-in-law and three children.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Would you now please tell the judges very briefly about some of the events that you observed in your village in the days and weeks leading up to 16th April 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In 1992, the first conflict occurred. I was 16, I was in eighth grade, after I completed eighth grade, I could not go to secondary school because of these reasons. Around September, November, the former Serbo-Croat was eliminated, nowadays it is called Bosnian; then we had the Croatian language. After that, there were not any significant changes until that date, 16th April 1993. There were not any major changes. We led a normal life.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: If I can just interrupt for a minute and clarify, you were explaining about the changes that occurred to the school system. Did you not return to school because the programme had changed and now they were forcing everyone to speak the Croatian language and to follow a curriculum that was based on Croatian culture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they required all to embrace the Croatian language. The new school year was supposed to be based on the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So for the school year of 1992, running into 1993, you did not attend school at all, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not want to accept the Croatian language, so I had no opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: In the days and weeks leading up to 16th April 1993, did you see any military activity in the area, did you see any men in uniform, did you see any troops in the area of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the neighbourhood. They wore their uniforms. They belonged to the HVO and they wore HVO insignia on their arms. First of all I would encounter Dragan Papic more often, who would go by often.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Was Mr. Papic a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please show the witness previously introduced exhibit number 100/2? I believe that is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness L, could you please come a little closer to the microphone? It is hard for the interpreters to hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Witness L, the usher has put a picture of a patch on the ELMO. Can you see it on your monitor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Does that patch resemble the HVO patches that you saw the soldiers wearing in Ahmici in 1992/1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but there are some differences, I mean there are some things that are missing on this patch, that are not displayed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: What is it that is missing? What did you see that was different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the right-hand corner and the left-hand corner, there were two crossed rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So in the area below the yellow circle and above the HVO, you saw two crossed guns, is that what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, we are finished with that exhibit. Now, Witness L, prior to 16th April 1993, were any members of your family involved in the Territorial Defence in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Would you tell the court who in your family was involved and what their responsibilities were within the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My father and my brother, my uncle. Naturally they went on guard only. They did not have enough -- I mean they did not have the right kind of guns or anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: As part of their responsibilities within the Territorial Defence, were they given weapons or did they already have weapons at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not get weapons, they had these weapons, they got it from the front-line and then they would readjust them, but you could not even do that properly, well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: You said earlier that your father and brother were living with you in April 1993, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Were they both members of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Did they both have weapons that they kept with them in your house?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson, the father and the brother were part of the Territorial Defence, we have already heard these questions and answers, I believe, so please do try to move forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Did your father and brother have guns that they kept in the house that they used when they worked with the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not have guns, I mean both of them, they both used the same weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Would you now please tell the court about the events that happened on the late night of 15th April and the early morning of 16th April 1993, to you and your family in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On 15th April, we were sitting at home as usual, watching television, and naturally we all went to sleep. On 16th April in the morning, around 5.30 or 6.00, first my mother got up and she started crying and that is how she woke up the rest of us, who were still asleep. I got up like my older sisters, we went out to see what was going on, what had happened. There was shooting coming from all over. There was a lot of smoke all around. Then I took the key of the summer storage, where we would leave fruit and vegetables for the winter. I went to unlock it to take a blanket there and foam mattresses so if necessary that we could seek shelter there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Approximately how far was this cellar, what I will refer to as the vegetable cellar, from your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is about 50 to 80 metres away from the house, it is within the compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: When you went to the cellar at that time, did you go by yourself or did other members of your family go with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went there on my own.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the cellar, and continue to tell the court what happened that morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed there for about half an hour, an hour up there. I could not get out straight away because when I got up there it was cold because the floor is concrete. It took me time to get dressed, to go to my sister and my mother and my father. I went out and I saw that the other houses were on fire, I saw the fire, I saw the flames, I did not dare go out, there was shooting from all over.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: You said that you could hear gunfire. Did there seem to be any gunfire close to where you were in the cellar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay. So you stayed in the cellar because you were afraid to leave because of all the shooting that was going on, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay, but at some point in time did you then return to the main house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Would you explain to the court what happened when you went back to the main house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came to the house I started having breakfast. My sisters, my mummy and my sister-in-law were terrified, they started crying because they saw through the window what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So at some point in time, did you and your family make a decision that you needed to leave your main house and go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we went back to the vegetable cellar again, where I was on my own before that. We went back there because we thought it was safer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: When you say "we", who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I meant my family, my mother, father, my sisters, my aunt, my uncle, my sister-in-law with her children.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So all those people then went to this vegetable cellar near the house, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: How long did you all stay in the vegetable cellar at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not stay very long, we stayed only for a short while, 15 minutes to half an hour, because it was not safe there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Why was it not safe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because there was more and more fire all over the village. After that, we could not find a way out, we could not get out. None of us could get out then. Then we would stay there and what would happen then?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay, so at some point in time, did you make a decision that you then needed to leave this vegetable cellar and go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay, would you tell the court what happened when you decided to leave the cellar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we set out, we decided to get out of there, to leave. There was no other way out. We went through the forest, which went through that area. Behind our backs was the house of Vlatko Kupreskic. From there we heard cursing, provocations. Then, after what they said, these curses, these provocations, then bursts of gunfire started, so they were shooting at us. Fortunately the first burst of gunfire did not harm anyone. I lay down immediately. The second burst of gunfire hit my mother, who was shot dead. The second burst of gunfire got me. My leg, the bullet went through the bone in two places, so I had two wounds on that leg. Below my knee and above my knee.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a couple of questions before you continue. You said that as you were running away from the cellar, you went through the woods for a distance and then you heard some people shouting at you, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Could you tell where these people were, where this sound was coming from, the people that were shouting at you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the house of Vlatko Kupreskic, because only his house was behind us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay, and during the time that you were running from the cellar until the point you and your mother were hit, was there constant gunfire around you or when you got to a certain point, did the gunfire start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only when we got to a certain point, a certain place, that is when they started shooting at us directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: At this time, Mr. Registrar, I would ask the usher to show the witness Exhibit 139, which has been premarked as 139. Copies have been provided to Defence counsel and to the judges. Would you just give that to the witness and not put it on the ELMO, please? Witness L, this is an enlargement of an aerial photograph and you have seen this exhibit before, have you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: The judges and Defence counsel have a copy of this so they can follow along. Can you just explain what is marked number 1 on this exhibit? What does that represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay, so the area that is circled and marked by number 1 is the approximate location of your house, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: What is represented by number 2X on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the place where this fruit and vegetable cellar is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay, and what is represented by number 3 on the diagram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the house of Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay, what is represented by number 4 on the diagram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The place of these events, the place of the wounding.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So number 4 is the approximate location where you were shot and where your mother was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay. If you could set aside the photograph for the time being, we will refer back to it in a few moments. Thank you. You said when you reached a certain point, as you were running through this field, you heard some bursts of gunfire, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: In one of the first bursts of gunfire your mother was shot, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: From where you were located, were you actually able to see your mother shot, were you able to see her hit and fall down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because it happened right next to me, maybe five or six steps away from me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Do you know, could you tell from where you were whether your mother died instantly or whether it took some time for her to die?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My sister was in front of her and I was behind her. My sister just cried out and she said, "mummy is dying", and she fell down, and then after that, after some time, I managed to get really close to her.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Were you able to see yourself the fact that your mother was dead or did someone inform you of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was able to see myself, because shortly after that I managed to get close to her, so I could see her.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay, and then it was shortly after your mother was shot that you were also shot, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, how shall I put it, it was just one burst of gunfire after the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Were you able to tell from what direction the gunfire was coming?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the house of Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: From where you were located, were you able to see anyone shooting at you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had our backs turned to them, we did not dare turn around, because we were just trying to save ourselves. But that was the only house behind us, his house.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So basically you concluded the gunfire was coming from Vlatko Kupreskic's house because you could hear it coming from direction but you could not necessarily see anyone shooting, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Again referring to exhibit number 139, number 3 on that exhibit is the house of Vlatko Kupreskic and number 4 is the location where you were shot, is that correct, again looking at the aerial photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay. Would you now continue to tell the court what happened after you were shot? What events transpired after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Next to me there was only my father, he was two steps away from me, below me, so he started dragging me by my legs in order to shelter me. Then he went over to my mother and he took her in his lap, and at that moment, one of our neighbours happened to pass by. I do not know how to say, but he was a very kind man, he helped me. He shouted at me, and he came quickly, he came running over to me, and he asked me what had happened to me, and I told him I had been wounded. Then first he went over to my mother and my father, and he realised that my mother was dead and at that moment I was next to my mother and I saw her. Then this neighbour told my father to let her go, that she was dead, and that they had to help me, and then my father told him to help me and that he would come shortly, so I went with him, with this neighbour. Shortly after that, my father joined us, and they helped me move out from that place, but we just managed to get just a little bit further. Then my uncle took over.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt for a moment and ask a couple of questions. After those first two or three bursts of gunfire when you and your mother were hit, did the gunfire continue or did it stop at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it continued in the area, but it was not aimed directly at us any longer. My sisters and my sister-in-law managed to escape, to find shelter, but we could still hear the shooting somewhere around.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: When the shooting was going on, was it just you and your family that was in that field, or did you see other people from the village in the area as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well my family was there and together with us there was a man with his wife and child, actually some elderly people who were from Prjedor and one more family that was with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: You said that among your family members with you that day were the children of your brother and sister-in-law, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: What were the approximate ages of those children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The eldest son was two years old, two and a half years old approximately, and the daughter could have been between a year and a year and a half years old, and the third child, a daughter, was very small, she could have been maybe not even a year -- she could not walk.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So those three children were with you and the rest of the family when you were in the field, when those bursts of gunfire were going on around you, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: But other than you and your mother, was anyone else from your family struck by any of the bullets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my family, no, but there was this neighbour who was with us and he was hit in the neck by a burst of gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay, now you said that after it became apparent that your mother had died, that your father and a neighbour came and helped you. Could you then tell the court what happened after they came to help you? Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am just trying to but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Just take your time. After you were shot and injured, you said that your father came to you and a neighbour came to you to help you. I assume that you could not walk because of your injuries, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay, so what did your father and this other man do, did they help you get away from that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Yes, they helped me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay, please tell the court where they took you and how they were able to help you get away from that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My father took me from one side by my arm and the neighbour helped me on the other side and then very slowly I could walk on one leg, but the other leg was hit directly in the bone. So we went over to a shelter, to the house, the house where we had found shelter before, I mean the house where we were supposed to find shelter, so while he was carrying me -- it was actually my uncle who took me over, and then after him it was my neighbour, one neighbour from Prjedor who helped me to get closer to the house, to climb over the fence. So that is how they carried me to the house, and I lay down on the mattress and they were trying to help me. They tried to stop the bleeding, because I was bleeding heavily.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay, could you describe to the court what the situation was in the house where they took you? Were there other people there? Can you just describe in general what the conditions were like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the house there were some girls, some women with children, some elderly women as well, whoever had managed to come there from the road, people who had managed to find shelter there. There was a large room in that house where there was water pipe and there was a small corridor and another room where they bandaged my wounds, where they gave me first aid.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Do you have any idea approximately how many other people were at this house that they took you to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how to put it, how to explain that, because people were coming one by one, trying to find shelter there, because -- people were coming from the lower part of the village, those who had managed to escape.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So did it appear that people were coming from all different parts of Ahmici, from the different villages around Ahmici and they all seemed to be gathering at this same approximate location, at this house where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were many refugees there, refugees from Karaula, Turbe, Jajce. Most of them were people from our area, people who had come from the main road up to the house, so that is the distance I am talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: All the people that were at this house where you were taken, were they all Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: You and your family, were you Muslims as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: When you were in the field and the bullets were being shot at you, were the other people with you in the field Muslims? Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not quite clear to me what field you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: I am referring to the field where you were shot and where your mother was killed, when there were those bursts of gunfire there. The other people that were with you who were also being shot at, were they also Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, together with me there were some Muslims, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay. Witness L, I would like to direct your attention again to exhibit number 139, the aerial photograph that is on the table in front of you. Would you just look at that again for a moment? Is the area marked by number 5 encircled, does that represent the approximate area of the house where you were taken after you were shot, the house you have just described where these other people were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Just to clarify, number 4 is the approximate location where you were shot, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, approximately. This is the distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please not too many repetitions, Ms. Paterson. It has already been said, and also primarily for the witness's own sake.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Witness L, would you continue to tell the court what happened when you were taken to this house. You said they administered some first aid. What basically happened after you got to that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They transferred me to another room, where other wounded people were placed, other women and children, and also other villagers from Ahmici, and then in about two or three hours maybe, even four, I do not remember exactly what time it was, I was bleeding heavily, and in the meantime, UNPROFOR arrived, they got to the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of approximately what time it was when UNPROFOR came to the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately, as far as I could tell, I think it could have been 1.00, 1.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Do you have any idea approximately what time it was that you were shot and that your mother was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It must have been around 8.00 -- between 7.30 and 9.00. It is difficult for me to tell you precisely at what time it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So between 7.30 and 9.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you think this is really that relevant, Ms. Paterson?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. President, yes, I do. I would not be asking the questions if I did not think they were important. We just have a little bit more testimony to go and then I will be asking you to go into the short private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine, I can go along with that, but still you have to see things in a relative light. You have to bear the purpose in mind. This is not an investigation into the unfortunate death of the mother of the witness, so please, it is just a matter of sticking to the essentials. So maybe Witness L could go on with her narrative and then you could go on with clarifications also because it is quite an ordeal for the witness, so please, from the arrival of UNPROFOR, could you go on and tell us in your own words what happened thereafter. Please proceed, Witness L.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will. When UNPROFOR came to the house where we were staying they got in immediately. They came to the room where we were and they dressed our wounds, to me and to other wounded persons who were there in the same room with me. Again they administered first aid, and then they took us to their APCs, which then transported us to Bila, where UNPROFOR had its own hospital. Again, they gave us medical help and we were given infusions, some injections, they took X-rays of the fractures and so on, so we stayed there until about 6.00, and again UNPROFOR took us to the hospital in Travnik and that is where we were admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: How long did you have to stay in the hospital after you were admitted? Altogether how long did you stay in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed there at Travnik hospital about 20 days and then after I was transferred to Zenica, to the hospital in Zenica, where I stayed an additional -- for maybe a month or so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it is at this time that it would be appropriate to go into a short private session, because the questions I need to ask her might in some ways identify who this witness is, so probably just a five or ten minute session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objection on the part of the Defence, I take it. So at the request of the parties, we are going to have a private session, so Witness L, you will still be subject to the very strict protective measures we have taken and in addition, we will be in camera, as it were, so that you may speak even more freely and you will not endanger anyone. Please, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go right ahead. This is an open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Good evening, Witness L, my name is Anto Nobilo and together with my colleague Russell Hayman, I am defending General Blaskic. I would like to put a few questions to you. We are in open session once again and there are not going to be any questions related to your person. Do you understand what I am saying? You do not need interpretation. What language am I speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You understand Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, you had two older sisters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did they go to secondary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did they go on to secondary school in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992 my sister, the one after me, the older sister of us all, I mean, she had finished school a long time ago, I mean before all of this. Then the other sister finished in 1990, when I finished eighth grade and she completed fourth grade of elementary school then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So why did you not want to go to school then when they changed the name of the language, because you did not understand it or was it a way of protest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I could not accept it myself, the Croat language, when I could not go to school on my own, my generation and the people before us, they did not want to accept that language.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it the same language or is it another language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean this Croat language.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You think that these are two languages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I mean it is similar, but I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But it is not the same language?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, the witness has answered your question. You are not going to go into an in-depth discussion about the differences between the two languages. Please move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I apologise, I am sorry. I am always upset when young people are indoctrinated, but that is not the subject of this trial. Tell me, you told me that your father and brother were in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do not jump to any premature conclusions. We are not interested in your opinions for the time being, sir. Go ahead with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, I just wish to recall the following. The witness said her father and brother were in the Territorial Defence, so I am putting the following question. Your brother and father, did they perhaps move into the BH army while you were in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The BH army, I mean it was not established just like that while we were still in Ahmici. They were only established later as the army, then they were still the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was not your brother a policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only afterwards he got that rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Not a rank, was your brother on the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that he was in the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So not before these events, these events of 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some time around the 16th or 17th, that is when he accepted I think to be on the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the day of April 16th, was your brother a member of the police force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On 15th April, was he in the police force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the exact day when he joined.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The night between 15th and 16th April, was your brother at home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends which duties they all had where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where was your brother assigned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where, as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I was not in Vitez, I could not tell where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So the night between 15th and the 16th, your brother was not with you, he was in Vitez assigned as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was that the first night that he was not with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean, was that the first night?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was it the first time that he went on duty to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. To tell you the truth, I did not understand all of that very well, I did not know about all of that, I was a child, I was too young to know all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me remind you, at the time of the events, the witness was all of 16, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am just asking whether any other night before the 15th her brother was out of the house on duty, that is all. If you remember, fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How can I remember? We lived in one part of the house and he -- I mean downstairs. He had his family that he took care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before, you told the investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor: "My brother was a policeman in Stari Vitez and he was not at home on the night between the 15th and 16th." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I said that he was in the police, but when he joined the police, I tell you, I was very young and I do not think I understood very seriously what it was all about, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were in this vegetable cellar, you said that shooting was coming from all over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell me from what directions most of the shooting came? Was shooting coming from all sides literally, or from upper Ahmici or lower Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The shoots were ringing out from the entrance to Ahmici, what we call lower Ahmici, and also from Zume and also from way up from upper Ahmici, I mean it is all around.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So in lower Ahmici, from Zume and from upper Ahmici. Tell me, when Vlatko Kupreskic was cursing your family, did you see his face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not say that, I said it was coming from his house. I am not claiming it was him exactly, because his house was behind my back. I did not see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But did you recognise his voice or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I really was not up to it. I did not feel like recognising voices, because I was trying to save my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you only know that it was coming from his house. At the moment when you were shot, when you were wounded --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: -- which direction were you facing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But where, were you facing upper Ahmici or some other direction when you were wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is a bit of a complicated question, is it not, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It takes a bit of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: She was 16, she was wounded; four years later she is being asked which way she was facing; that may be just a wee bit complicated, do you not think?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I agree, but I have to try. If she can recollect, fine, but if she cannot ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How can I remember, I was lying --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: If you cannot remember, it is all right, let us go on. I agree. When you came to upper Ahmici, were there any HVO soldiers there, did you see them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not go up there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you came to the shelter, before you came to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before I came to the shelter, how should I put this, this was my neighbourhood and the women and children were protected, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So it was only Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I could not see further on because I was carried there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So who protected these women and children? Who did you see protecting the women and children out of the Muslims who had weapons? Who was protecting the shelter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean, who did I see and who was protecting them?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you see any Muslims armed with weapons, one of your neighbours, protecting women and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were standing near that house, but they did not have enough weapons and all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who was standing there with not enough weapons? Do you remember the names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I do not know how to put this, all of this was very fast and my leg was bleeding, you know, I was being moved from one set of hands to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You know there was someone who was there protecting you with not enough weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but there were too few people, five or six people. There were four people who were taking me over, one after another and the fifth one carried me in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your uncle, did he have weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My uncle had a rifle with a twisted barrel, I mean, it had been fired before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And the neighbour from Prjedor, did he have weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: While you were in the shelter --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: -- did you hear gunfire from your immediate vicinity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Naturally you could hear shooting until UNPROFOR came. When UNPROFOR came, then things went quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And the wounded who were in the shelter, were they men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were three of us there, an older man, really older, and another one was somewhat younger, so it was two men and me only, so while I was still there, there was three of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were there any beds in this shelter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Stretchers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, blankets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Blankets. Did you have iodine, bandages and first aid equipment and kits?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were very few bandages. They even had to put wax paper on my wounds so that I would not spoil so many bandages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. (Pause). Thank you, Mr. President, we have thus concluded our questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson, is there something you would like to add.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, very briefly. Just two questions. Witness L, I believe Mr. Nobilo said during his questioning of you that your brother was a soldier on duty in Vitez. Was your brother a soldier or was he a policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was only that he -- I mean I did not quite understand the events, but it was only after that he became a policeman, a civilian policeman. I mean after that, after he went -- I do not know how he went to Vitez and how he ended up there. I do not quite understand what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: But on 16th April, is it your understanding that your brother was a policeman in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well first he was like -- as far as I can remember, first he was like a soldier and then later, I do not know when, he went to Vitez or maybe it was before that, I do not remember exactly. He was a military policeman and then after that, he joined the civilian police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So when you are saying he was a military policeman, was this when he did his mandatory JNA service, or was this in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1993, I think that -- no, in 1992 he was a simple soldier, he was wounded in the spinal area, so he had some privileges and then he joined the police force, I mean the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay. Just one other thing, you said that when you were at the shelter after you had been wounded when UNPROFOR came, it got very quiet. Can you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I meant to say, I think the HVO stopped shooting while UNPROFOR was there, and, of course, after UNPROFOR left, I left with them, so I do not know what happened after that. I do not know whether they continued or what happened, because I left with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me turn to fellow judges. Judge Riad, do you have some questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, I will call you Witness L, as you know. No names should be mentioned. Please feel free to answer any question or not to answer, because, of course, you were quite young when these events happened. But I think you are sufficiently conscious of what is happening, so at least you can answer some questions. What was the majority of the people living in Ahmici? Were they Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Were they divided in the village or in the town, sections for the Muslims and sections where the Croats are living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well in the lower part -- near the mosque, there were only Muslims, and in the other part of the village, the population was mixed, Muslims and Croats, so from the upper mosque, there were only Muslims and below the mosque, the population was mixed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: When you left school in 1992, you left it as a protest against the change of curriculum and that you said they changed the language and the culture. What do you mean by the change of culture? What was the culture taught in the schools and what was it changed into? Did you understand what it was about when you took this decision? Did they try to completely avoid or discard the Bosniak culture or the Muslim traditions? What happened exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do not know what was happening exactly, but I mean I do not know how to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: All right. Now when you were shot at and your mother was shot at, I noted that you mentioned that, even I wrote your sentence, translated to English: "There was one burst of gunfire after the other, coming from the direction of Vlatko Kupreskic's house." So Vlatko Kupreskic's house was a Croat house, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Was the shooting aimed at you specifically or was it just shooting at anybody that was moving there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment, nobody was moving except for us, and we were all standing close to each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Because you said your sister and her small children and other man and wife of the child, all of them were either killed or wounded and so on, so you were all in one group and the group was shot at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Women and children and everything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we had set out together and they started cursing us, it was coming from Vlatko Kupreskic's house, and then at that moment we were trying to escape and at that moment I lay down on the ground, and while I was lying down on the ground, my leg was bent and that is how the burst of gunfire caught me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Was your brother with you at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: He was not with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: You mentioned that he was in the military police. Which military police was that? Do you know, was it the BH, was it the Yugoslav army before? What was that? What is the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was this BH, I mean they were manning the checkpoints. I do not know what exactly they were, I just know that it was the BH, but I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Was he engaged in any fight with Vlatko Kupreskic or with anybody from the Croat community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in the neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: When you spoke of when your grandfather and grandmother died and were burnt alive in the house, you said that they died or they were burnt alive because they remained behind when other people left and as you said exactly, you said that the HVO came to set fire on the remaining houses which remained after the exodus and after the firing. Is that, according to you, there was a plan to burn all the Muslim houses, this is why they returned to finish them up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what kind of plan they had in mind, but they had intentions, I mean that day, judging from the area around while I was still there, there were houses that were on fire and while I was still there, I saw some -- I saw actually quite a few houses that had been burnt down. I even passed by some houses that --

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: You said they returned after that, after you left to make sure that all the houses were burnt; that is what I understood. Is that what you meant when your grandfather was burnt alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not my grandfather, my grandfather was killed, he had come back to my mother's body, where she remained. That is where he was killed, on that spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Then who were the grandparents who were there when they came to burn the houses? I noted down that, the grandparents and an uncle.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could interrupt for just a moment, could we possibly go off the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What is the reason to go off the record?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to bring to the court's attention that Judge Riad is venturing into an area that was some of the testimony that we dealt with in the private session. That was part of the reason for doing it in the private session, was to keep some of this information confidential. I would just like to bring that to your attention and ask you to be careful in how the questions are framed so we do not inadvertently identify anyone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I fully realise that, but I think many people have got grandparents, so I do not think this is a secret. I think I have finished, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine, now I do not have any questions either, so Witness L, you have done quite well. What is your health like now, it is good, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am not going to ask you what you are up to, because we do not want to identify you in any way. You are young, you were young at the time of these great sufferings, and all we can do is to hope that your life will be fulfilled in the future. Now I think we are going to adjourn. There are no further witnesses this afternoon, are there, Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, there are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Right. That was why we did not have a recess. This session is closed and we are going to resume Monday at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: on Monday, 24th November 1997)
